en: The Discourse on Dependent Origination and the Noble Path, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove.

At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as an immeasurable multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"Before I had realized unexcelled perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), while dwelling alone in a secluded place, sitting in silent tranquility, I gave rise to this thought:
'How extraordinary!'"
The world is submerged in the ocean of suffering, yet none perceive the Dharma for transcendence; this is truly to be pitied.
For although there is birth, aging, and death—passing away from here and being born there—sentient beings are unable to know, as it truly is, the Dharma for transcending birth, aging, and death.
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what does aging and death come to be?
By what condition, furthermore, does such aging and death arise?"
When I reflected upon this matter as it truly is, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because birth exists, aging and death exist;
thus, aging and death have birth as their condition."
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what does birth come to be?
By what condition, moreover, does such birth arise?"
When I reflected on this matter according to reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because existence exists, birth comes to be;
such birth has existence as its condition."
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what does 'existence' (bhava) come to be?
By what condition, moreover, does such existence arise?"
When I reflected on this matter as it truly is, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because of the existence of grasping (*upādāna*), there is the existence of becoming (*bhava*).
Thus, becoming has grasping as its condition."
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what is there grasping?
By what condition does such grasping arise?"
When I reflected on this matter as it truly is, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because craving exists, grasping comes to be;
thus, grasping has craving as its condition."
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what does craving come to be?
By what condition, moreover, does such craving arise?"
When I reflected on this matter as it truly is, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because of feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) comes to be;
such craving has feeling as its condition."
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what is there feeling?
From what condition does such feeling arise?"
When I reflected on this matter as it truly is, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because contact exists, feeling comes to be;
such feeling has contact as its condition."
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what does contact arise?
From what condition does such contact arise?"
When I reflected upon this matter in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct contemplation of things as they truly are:
"Because the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be;
such contact has the six sense bases as its condition."
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what do the six sense bases come to be?
By what condition, moreover, do these six sense bases arise?"
When I reflected upon this matter in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct contemplation of things as they truly are:
"With name-and-form, the six sense bases come to be;
thus, the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition."
I further reflected:
"Due to the existence of what is there name-and-form?
By what condition does such name-and-form arise?"
When I reflected upon this matter as it truly is, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because consciousness exists, name-and-form come to be;
thus, name-and-form have consciousness as their condition."
“At this point my consciousness turns back and does not proceed further, thinking:
‘With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form;
with name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases.’”
With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact;
with contact as condition, feeling;
with feeling as condition, craving.
With craving as condition, grasping arises;
with grasping as condition, becoming arises;
with becoming as condition, birth arises.
With birth as condition, there arise aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, affliction, and despair.
In this way, there is the accumulation of this entire great mass of suffering.
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what is there no aging and death?
Through the cessation of what does aging and death subsequently cease?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because there is no birth, there is no aging and death.
With the cessation of birth, aging and death cease accordingly."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what is there no birth?
Through the cessation of what does this birth subsequently cease?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"Because existence does not exist, birth does not exist;
through the cessation of existence, birth accordingly ceases."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what does existence not come to be?
Through the cessation of what does this existence subsequently cease?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct contemplation as it truly is:
"Because there is no grasping, there is no becoming;
through the cessation of grasping, becoming itself ceases."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what is there no grasping?
Through the cessation of what does this grasping cease accordingly?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"In the absence of craving, grasping does not exist;
through the cessation of craving, grasping likewise ceases."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what does craving not exist?
Through the cessation of what does this craving subsequently cease?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"In the absence of feeling, craving does not exist;
through the cessation of feeling, craving likewise ceases."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what is there no feeling?
Through the cessation of what does this feeling subsequently cease?"
As I reflected on this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"In the absence of contact, there is no feeling;
through the cessation of contact, feeling likewise ceases."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what is there no contact?
Through the cessation of what does this contact subsequently cease?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"In the absence of the six sense bases, contact does not exist;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact likewise ceases."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what do the six sense bases not exist?
Through the cessation of what do the six sense bases cease accordingly?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"In the absence of name-and-form, the six sense bases do not exist;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease accordingly."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what do name-and-form not exist?
Through the cessation of what does name-and-form cease?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"In the absence of consciousness, name-and-form do not exist;
through the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease accordingly."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what is there no consciousness?
Through the cessation of what does this consciousness subsequently cease?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"In the absence of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not exist;
through the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness likewise ceases."
I further reflected:
"In the absence of what do volitional formations not exist?
By the cessation of what do these volitional formations cease?"
As I reflected upon this in accordance with reality, there arose in me this direct realization:
"In the absence of ignorance, volitional formations do not exist;
with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations likewise cease."
With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness also ceases;
with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease;
with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease.
With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact also ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling also ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving also ceases.
With the cessation of craving, grasping also ceases;
with the cessation of grasping, becoming also ceases;
with the cessation of becoming, birth also ceases.
With the cessation of birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, agitation, and despair likewise cease.
In this way, this entire mass of pure suffering is utterly extinguished.
I further reflected:
"I have now realized the ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient course of conduct, that which was traversed by the seers of antiquity."

"It is, for example, as if a person were wandering through a wilderness, a perilous and foul thicket, when suddenly they encounter an old road, an old path, an old track traversed in the past by people of former times."
He immediately set out on his journey.
Having traveled, he beheld an ancient city, a royal capital of former times, complete with gardens, groves, and ponds; its pure and wondrous streets were most delightful.
Having seen this, the man thought to himself:
"I should now go quickly to the king's presence and report this matter.
Thereupon, the man went to the king's presence and addressed him, saying:
"Great King, you should know this:

I had occasion to wander through a wilderness, a rugged and foul thicket, when I suddenly encountered an ancient road, an ancient path, an ancient track, one formerly traversed by people of antiquity."
I immediately set out on my journey.
Having traveled, I beheld an ancient city and a former royal capital, complete with gardens, groves, and ponds, its pure and wondrous streets most delightful to behold.
"Great King!
If you now establish your capital in that city, it will surely cause Your Majesty to flourish and expand, remaining secure, prosperous, and joyful, with the population increasing and thriving."
At that time, the king established his capital in that city.
Later, the royal capital became prosperous and vast, peaceful and abundant, with a flourishing population.
"I too am thus.
Now I have realized the ancient path, the ancient track, the ancient course of conduct, that which was formerly traversed by the seers of old."
What is called the ancient road, the ancient path, the ancient track, and that which was formerly traversed by the seers of old?

It should be known as the Noble Eightfold Path: namely, first, right view; followed by right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, up to the eighth.
This is called the ancient road, the ancient path, the ancient track, the one traversed by the seers of old.
In the past, I followed it;
having followed it, I saw aging-and-death, I saw the origin of aging-and-death, I saw the cessation of aging-and-death, and I saw the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death.

In this way, he has previously seen birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, and volitional formations; he has previously seen the arising of volitional formations, the cessation of volitional formations, and the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations.
Having spontaneously attained mastery over this Dharma and realized perfect enlightenment,
I have declared it to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as to the vast multitude of various outsiders, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and other types of renunciants.
If these bhikṣus are able to practice correctly within this and achieve realization, they will be able to realize the excellence of the Dharma of the True Principle.

If the great assemblies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās are able to practice correctly within this and achieve realization, they will be able to realize the excellence of the Dharma of the True Principle.

"In this way, one is able to expand and broaden the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and shall likewise bring benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, providing correct and skillful instruction for all devas and humans.

At that time, the great assembly of bhikṣus, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; they were all filled with great joy, and with faith and acceptance, they put it into practice.
The Discourse on the Noble Path of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda Ariyamagga Sutta)
